protocol.name: qdwin_shell_v1
protocol.description:
Private protocol between the qdwin compositor and the qdistro PyQt shell. The shell connects as a normal Wayland client (same display socket), but qdwin only advertises this global to clients whose peer credentials (uid, exe, SELinux label) match the admin- configured shell identity — regular app clients never see it.
The protocol carries two streams:
- Toplevel lifecycle events from the compositor to the shell. For every xdg-toplevel qdwin tracks, the shell receives added / moved / state / focus / title / removed events. The shell uses this to draw window chrome (close / minimise / maximise buttons and the per-user-colour isolation border, per the architecture doc §4).
- Chrome buffer attachments from the shell to the compositor. The shell renders the decoration pixels into standard wl_buffers and attaches them per toplevel side; qdwin composites them around the toplevel's content surface via weston_view.
All user actions on the chrome (clicking close, dragging the title bar to move, clicking minimise) flow back from the shell as request_* messages. The compositor applies policy (lock state, rate limiting) before issuing the corresponding xdg-toplevel op. This keeps qdwin authoritative over window state — a crashed or compromised shell cannot directly act on a client.
No-shell-fallback rule: until the shell has sent `bind_as_shell` and acknowledged a toplevel (by calling either `set_border_color` or `attach_decoration` for it), qdwin does NOT composite that toplevel to any output. The client runs and queues frames, but is invisible. See the architecture doc §Bootstrap.
Warning! The protocol described in this file is experimental and pre-stable. Breaking changes may happen. Versioning follows the "experimental" convention: version 1 is the first unstable draft.

interface.name: qdwin_shell_v1
interface.description:
The shell binds this global once and holds it for the lifetime of its process. qdwin rejects a second bind from the same client; a new shell must replace the old one by first destroying its binding (via the standard wl_registry delete).
Version 2 adds seat and output lifecycle events (`seat_created` / `seat_removed` / `output_created` / `output_removed`). Shells that need to react to RDP-subscriber connect/disconnect or to output hot-plug should bind at ≥v2; v1 shells keep getting only toplevel-scoped events.
Version 13 adds `toplevel_security_context` so shells get the `(sandbox_engine, app_id, instance_id)` carried by a sandboxed client's `wp_security_context_v1` tag in-band rather than via the chrome-side title-prefix heuristic. v12 and earlier shells keep classifying sandboxed toplevels by title prefix.
Version 14 adds `seat_focus_changed` (event) and `set_keyboard_focus` (request). The event lets the shell react to keyboard-focus moves and implement spec/10 §"focus-aware selection clear" — when the focus moves to a different silo, the shell drops the seat selection so the newly focused client can't `wl_data_offer.receive` admin's clipboard. The request is the ctrl-socket-side test hook for headless bats coverage and for future click-to-focus on chrome.
Version 16 adds `set_keyboard_focus_v2` so the shell can pass the target toplevel's silo identity at focus-injection time. v14's unconditional `weston_seat_set_selection(NULL, fresh_serial)` on every set_keyboard_focus is correct for cross-silo moves (defense-in-depth) but kills the active selection on same-silo moves — which breaks the v15 sink-path: a sink-toplevel that takes focus on the same silo as a still-active source must receive the existing offer, not see a cleared selection. v2 tracks the last v2-focused silo per seat; if the new `target_silo` matches, the clear is skipped and the existing selection survives. v2 is purely additive — pre-v16 shells keep using `set_keyboard_focus` and get the v14 unconditional-clear behaviour.
Version 17 adds `overlay_key`, the keyboard-input route into the launcher / switcher / locker overlay surfaces. Until v17 the compositor never delivered key events to those surfaces — the shell could only drive them via its private ctrl-socket. With v17 the compositor installs a keyboard grab while an overlay is visible and forwards each press as `overlay_key(role, sym, utf8, state)`; the shell decodes utf8 for printable chars and matches `sym` (xkb keysym) for named keys (Escape, Return, Tab, arrows, Backspace). Pre-v17 shells stay on the ctrl-socket-only path.
Version 19 adds `register_hotkey` / `unregister_hotkey` / `hotkey_pressed` for shell-driven global keyboard shortcuts. The shell registers (linux-keycode + modifier-bitmask) tuples; the compositor installs a weston key-binding for each and emits `hotkey_pressed(id)` when the combo fires anywhere outside an active overlay grab. Used for Super+Space → launcher, Super+L → lock, etc. — any time a key combo should reach the shell without an existing overlay surface to take focus.
Version 18 adds `attach_background`: the shell registers a fullscreen wl_surface as the desktop background, replacing qdwin's compositor-owned `weston_curtain`. With a real client surface covering the desktop, two things become possible that were impossible before: (a) the shell calls `wl_pointer.set_cursor` on `wl_pointer.enter` over the background, so a default cursor sprite is always visible to SPICE / VNC viewers (the curtain was compositor-owned and never received pointer focus, so no client could set a cursor over empty desktop); (b) clicks on the empty desktop now have a target client to receive them. Pre-v18 shells continue with the compositor curtain.

entry.name: already_bound
entry.summary: shell has already claimed the shell role

entry.name: invalid_handle
entry.summary: toplevel handle does not exist or was removed

entry.name: locked
entry.summary: compositor is in locked state; request refused

entry.name: stream_unavailable
entry.summary: pipewire backend not loaded; per-view forwarding disabled

request.name: bind_as_shell
request.description:
The shell announces that it is ready to receive toplevel events and render decorations. Must be the first request on the interface after binding. qdwin replays any toplevels that already exist before this call as a burst of `toplevel_added` events — the shell must treat `bind_as_shell` as the point at which the event stream becomes live.
If this client has already called `bind_as_shell`, or if another client has, qdwin raises the `already_bound` error.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Release the shell binding. Any in-flight decoration buffers are detached. Toplevels revert to pending-chrome holding state until a fresh shell binds.

request.name: set_border_color
request.description: Record the isolation colour qdwin should associate with this toplevel — typically the colour of the uid the toplevel belongs to. The shell uses the same colour when painting the decoration buffer; the compositor uses it for any out-of-band rendering (e.g. focus ring during `begin_interactive_move`).

request.name: attach_decoration

description.summary: attach chrome surfaces to a toplevel

request.description:
Supply one wl_surface per side of the decoration frame. The shell client is expected to have created the wl_surface, attached a wl_buffer containing the decoration pixels, and committed before calling this request — otherwise the surface has no content and qdwin refuses the side. Passing NULL for a side leaves that edge undecorated.
qdwin creates an internal weston_view over each supplied surface and positions it flush against the toplevel content. The shell keeps ownership of the wl_surface and may update it by attaching new buffers + committing at any cadence; qdwin re-reads the surface on damage. To detach a side, pass NULL (the view is removed); to stop decorating entirely, destroy the wl_surface (qdwin observes the destroy and tears down its view).
Why wl_surface rather than wl_buffer: Weston's composition pipeline operates on surfaces, not bare buffers. A wl_surface carries the buffer, damage regions, scale, transform, and viewport as one atomic commit — matching the per-frame contract weston_view expects.
This is the point at which a toplevel transitions out of pending-chrome holding state. The first attach_decoration or set_border_color is what makes the client visible.

request.name: request_close

description.summary: user clicked close on the chrome

request.description: Forward a close request to the backing toplevel. qdwin calls `xdg_toplevel.close` after checking policy (not locked, not rate-limited).

description.summary: user raised the toplevel via chrome

request.name: begin_interactive_move
request.description: The shell reports the wl_pointer serial from the button press; qdwin enters its move-drag state machine. Tiled windows are refused (not an error — simply ignored); floating windows move with the pointer.

request.name: begin_interactive_resize
request.description: v1 note: qdwin accepts the request but may refuse non-floating toplevels. A future version will let the shell specify an edge mask so the cursor hint and constraint are correct.

request.name: show_popup
request.description:
Place `surface` as a popup anchored to toplevel `parent`, positioned at (x, y) in parent-local coordinates (the origin is the top-left of the parent's outer-rect, i.e. north-west of the N chrome).
The compositor creates a weston_view over `surface` on a popup layer above normal app windows and composites it there until the client destroys the returned `qdwin_popup_v1` object, or until the compositor dismisses it (pointer click outside, parent closed, compositor locked). Destroying the wl_surface also tears the popup down.
The shell is expected to have committed a buffer to `surface` before calling show_popup. Like chrome surfaces, popups are roleless wl_surfaces — no xdg_popup role is involved.
Only one popup is active per parent at a time. A second show_popup with the same parent dismisses the prior popup (the `dismissed` event fires on the old object before the new one becomes visible).

request.name: subscribe_view_stream

description.summary: start per-view forwarding of a toplevel

request.description:
Ask the compositor to forward toplevel `handle` as an out-of-band video stream (PipeWire today; RDP/PipeWire via qdistro-forward to remote clients). See the roadmap §6.5 and .
Admin approval is NOT done here. The shell is expected to have already resolved policy (qbus-admin `CheckPermission`, per the permissions doc §6.5 S4) before sending this request. qdwin trusts its bound shell — the shell is the policy layer, qdwin is compositor mechanics. A future non-shell caller would gate behind a separate allowed-uid check before reaching this code path.
On receipt, qdwin: 1. Validates `handle` is a live toplevel (else `invalid_handle`). 2. Validates the pipewire backend is loaded (else `stream_unavailable`). 3. Allocates a pipewire output via `weston_pipewire_output_api_v2.head_create`, pins the view to that output via `weston_view_set_output`, spawns a qdistro-forward child process that serves the stream to remote RDP clients, and emits `approved`. 4. On any failure (no free pipewire output, spawn error): emits `denied` with a diagnostic reason string.
`desired_width` and `desired_height` are hints for the output size; the compositor may clamp. `allow_input` is purely informational in this version — whether the subscriber may inject input is decided server-side by the admin approval and reflected in whether the compositor advertises `qdwin_stream_input_v1` to the matching qdistro-forward.
`peer_label` is a caller-chosen short string shown in the admin prompt ("Forward to phone", "Share with work").

arg.name: allow_input
arg.summary: hint: 0 read-only, 1 subscriber may inject input

event.name: hello

description.summary: bind accepted, carry back the server's view of the client

event.description: Emitted once immediately after a successful bind, before any `toplevel_added` replay. Carries the uid the compositor saw, so the shell can confirm its identity matches expectations.

event.name: toplevel_added
event.description:
Sent after the toplevel is mapped and ready for decoration. The toplevel is in pending-chrome holding state until the shell's first attach_decoration for this handle arrives.
`owner_uid` is the uid of the process that owns the backing wl_client. qdwin is the only party that can authoritatively attribute this — the threat-model doc; the shell uses it to pick the correct border colour, or to annotate the decoration with a debug label. A future version may replace this with an opaque colour token if the uid itself should not leak to the shell.

event.name: toplevel_state
event.description: State bitmask: bit 0 maximised, bit 1 fullscreen, bit 2 minimised, bit 3 urgent, bit 4 focused, bit 5 floating. More bits reserved.

event.name: toplevel_removed
event.description: The shell should release any wl_buffers it still holds for this handle. The handle is retired; a subsequent toplevel_added may reuse the numeric value but it refers to a different view.

event.name: locked_changed

description.summary: compositor entered or left locked state

event.description: While locked, qdwin refuses all request_* on the interface (raises `locked` error) and stops emitting per-toplevel events. The shell uses this to swap to the lock UI layer-shell surface.

event.name: seat_created
event.description:
Forwarded from `weston_compositor::seat_created_signal`. The qdwin source publishes one event per seat, including the seats that already exist at `bind_as_shell` time (replay).
Typical triggers: the initial libinput seat at compositor startup, a new RDP client connecting (the RDP backend creates a per-client seat), or a per-view seat spun up by `qdwin_stream_input_v1` for an active forward (§6.5 S5).
`name` is `weston_seat::seat_name` — opaque to the shell beyond use as a correlation key. Shells that care about the seat's kind (physical input vs. RDP vs. per-stream virtual) today infer it from the name prefix ("default", "rdp-", or "qdwin-stream-"); a future event field may formalise this.

event.name: seat_removed
event.description:
Forwarded from `weston_seat::destroy_signal`. Emitted once per seat at teardown. Pairs 1:1 with a prior `seat_created` for the same `name`.
Use cases: per-uid session-state cleanup when an RDP subscriber disconnects (§6.5), per-stream UI reset when the stream-input seat is released, and general diagnostic logging.

event.name: output_created
event.description:
Forwarded from `weston_compositor::output_created_signal`. Replayed at `bind_as_shell` for outputs that exist at bind time.
`name` is `weston_output::name` (e.g. "pipewire-1", "headless-0", or a DRM connector name). Shells may use it to label per-output UI or to correlate with pipewire node names exposed via `qdwin_view_stream_v1.approved`.

event.name: output_removed
event.description: Forwarded from `weston_compositor::output_destroyed_signal`. Pairs 1:1 with a prior `output_created`. Matters when hot- plug DRM outputs land and for pipewire outputs that get torn down as view streams end.

request.name: attach_panel

description.summary: promote a wl_surface to a panel role

request.description:
Requests that the compositor treat `surface` as a shell-owned panel. The compositor places the surface on its panel layer (above normal toplevels, below popups), anchors it to the given screen `edge`, and reserves an exclusive zone of `thickness` pixels so xdg-toplevel maximise does not cover the panel.
The returned `qdwin_panel_v1` handle mirrors the popup / stream handle pattern. Destroying the handle unmaps the panel and releases its exclusive zone. Multiple panels are allowed (one per edge per output); the compositor picks the primary output if the shell doesn't specify.
Shell must render continuously into `surface` (attach + damage + commit) and `set_border_color` rules don't apply — the panel carries its own chrome.

arg.name: thickness
arg.summary: panel thickness in px (height for top/bottom, width for left/right)

arg.name: exclusive
arg.summary: exclusive zone in px (usually == thickness; 0 to overlay without reserving)

request.name: attach_notification

description.summary: promote a wl_surface to a notification role

request.description:
Places `surface` on the notification layer, positioned at the given corner of the primary output plus (offset_x, offset_y) in px. The shell pre-paints the bubble at whatever size it wants (from the surface's committed buffer dims). Multiple notifications stack — the shell is responsible for offsetting each one so they don't overlap.
Destroying the handle unmaps the bubble. The compositor may also fire `dismissed` if the hosting output is removed.

arg.name: offset_x
arg.summary: px offset from anchored corner on the x axis

arg.name: offset_y
arg.summary: px offset from anchored corner on the y axis

request.name: attach_launcher

description.summary: promote a wl_surface to a launcher role

request.description:
Places `surface` on the launcher layer, centred on the primary output. `kind` distinguishes launcher (0) from task switcher (1) — both share the same role/layer, the shell decides the content. Destroying the handle unmaps.
Compositor fires `dismissed` on output loss or when Escape is pressed and the shell-side grab surfaces it. Keyboard focus stealing is shell-side — qdwin does not redirect input on attach; the shell should call begin_interactive_move or a future focus-grab request to pull focus.

event.name: launcher_requested
event.description: Fired when the compositor's Ctrl+Space global binding fires. The shell responds by attaching a launcher surface via attach_launcher. If a launcher is already attached, the shell should dismiss it (toggle).

event.name: switcher_next
event.description: Fired when the compositor's Alt+Tab global binding fires. `direction` is 1 for forward (Alt+Tab) and -1 for reverse (Alt+Shift+Tab). The shell attaches a switcher surface via `attach_launcher(..., kind=1)` on the first event and cycles on subsequent ones while Alt is held. The compositor fires `switcher_commit` on Alt release so the shell can commit the selection.

description.summary: alt key released; shell should commit the highlighted toplevel

request.name: attach_lock_surface
request.description: Places `surface` on the compositor LOCK layer, covering every output. The surface is not yet "live" — the lock state is still driven by `set_locked`. Multiple lock surfaces are not allowed; a second attach replaces the first and dismisses it.

request.name: set_locked
request.description:
`locked=1` → compositor enters the locked state: the lock surface (from attach_lock_surface) is the only thing composited. `locked=0` → unlocks; toplevels resume rendering.
Compositor emits `locked_changed(locked)` after the transition, matching the existing auto-emit on boot.
Fails silently if no lock surface is attached; the shell is responsible for attaching first.

event.name: lock_requested
event.description: Fired when the compositor's Ctrl+Alt+L global binding fires. The shell should respond by calling `attach_lock_surface` (if not already attached) + `set_locked(1)`. Compositor does not itself flip lock state — the shell decides, so that an auth panel can be shown before entering lock if desired.

event.name: overlay_key

description.summary: key forwarded into a visible overlay surface

event.description:
While an overlay surface (launcher / switcher / locker) is attached and visible, the compositor installs a keyboard grab and forwards each pressed key here. The shell handles input directly — there is no separate wl_keyboard.key delivery to the overlay surface (overlays are not focusable in the normal sense; this event IS the focus path).
`role` distinguishes the overlay: 0=launcher, 1=switcher, 2=locker. The shell ignores roles whose state machine isn't currently active.
`sym` is the xkb keysym (XKB_KEY_*); the shell matches against named keys (XKB_KEY_Escape, XKB_KEY_Return, XKB_KEY_BackSpace, XKB_KEY_Up, XKB_KEY_Down, XKB_KEY_Tab) for navigation / commit / dismiss. `utf8` is the printable character (or "" if non-printable) for typing into filter / password fields. The shell prefers utf8 when non-empty (so xkb layout dead-keys and Compose are honoured) and falls back to `sym` matching for control keys.
Only PRESSED transitions are sent (state=1). Releases are absorbed by the grab.
The compositor stops forwarding when the overlay surface is destroyed; on the next attach the grab is reinstalled.

event.name: idle_lock_hint
event.description:
Fired by the compositor when it detects an idle condition that the spec 04 Lock-triggers section enumerates as a lock source but the shell can't observe directly (e.g. lid close signal pre-aggregated by the compositor). The shell treats this like lock_requested. `reason` is one of 0=idle, 1=lid_close, 2=prepare_for_sleep, 3=manual for logging.
Idle based on ext-idle-notify-v1 subscription is observed by the shell *directly* via that protocol — this event is only fired for reasons that need compositor-side aggregation.

event.name: nested_proxy_pending

description.summary: a nested-compositor advertise needs admin gating

event.description:
Fired by the compositor when a qdwin_nested_v1 advertise_toplevel creates a proxy in pending state (held layer, invisible). The shell must call `nested_proxy_decision(handle, decision, reason)` within a reasonable window — until then, the proxy stays held.
Action string for broker CheckPermission convention: `qdistro.nested.advertise:<slug(app_id)>` Details dict should carry: app_id, title, origin_uid.
`handle` matches the toplevel_added event's handle that fired immediately before this. Shells that don't bind v8 don't get this event and proxies auto-allow (compositor's `QDWIN_NESTED_BROKER_REQUIRED=1` env can override to fail-closed).

request.name: nested_proxy_decision

description.summary: shell's verdict on a pending nested proxy

request.description:
Issued by the shell after broker CheckPermission returns. The compositor holds nested-proxy toplevels until this lands.
decision values: 0 — allow: release the proxy from held to normal layer; it becomes visible to the user. Subsequent attach_decoration wires chrome around it. 1 — deny: post wl_resource_post_error on the originating qdwin_nested_toplevel_v1 with code `policy_denied`, destroy the proxy, and forget the handle. The nested compositor sees the protocol error and tears down its local PipeWire output for this toplevel. 2 — defer: keep the proxy held; shell may re-decide later (e.g. once admin approves a pending policy-change request the broker enqueued). No auto-timeout — the proxy lives until the resource closes or another decision arrives.
`reason` is a free-form string for audit logging; passed to the compositor log when posting the protocol error.
Calling this on a non-pending or unknown handle is a silent no-op (shells may issue stale decisions if a nested compositor teardown raced a broker call).

request.name: bind_proxy_pixels

description.summary: bind a wl_surface as the pixel source for a nested-proxy

request.description:
Tell the compositor that `surface` should be the pixel source for nested-proxy `handle`. Issued by the admin shell after it receives `nested_proxy_pixel_source` and successfully spawns a consumer process that has connected back, created its own wl_surface, and started feeding pixels into it.
On success the compositor swaps the placeholder curtain view for a weston_view of `surface`, places the new view on the normal layer at the same position, maps the surface so commits are composited, and sets the surface's destroy listener so the proxy reverts to a placeholder curtain if the consumer exits.
Issuing this on a non-existent or non-proxy `handle` raises `invalid_handle`.

event.name: nested_proxy_pixel_source

description.summary: metadata the shell needs to spawn a pixel consumer

event.description:
Fired by the compositor immediately after `nested_proxy_pending` for the same handle (so the shell can correlate). Carries the `pw_node` string from the original `qdwin_nested_v1.advertise_ toplevel` call; the shell uses it to spawn a consumer process (e.g. `qdistro-nested-pixelfeed`) that will resolve the node via libpipewire and call `bind_proxy_pixels`.
`input_sink` is forwarded too in case the shell wants a single consumer process to drive both the pixel feed and the input injection encoder; in normal operation those concerns are independent (input is the compositor's pointer-grab path, S3b).
For pre-v9 shells this event isn't sent; proxies stay in placeholder-curtain mode until a v9 shell is bound.

request.name: set_cursor_sprite

description.summary: provide a wl_surface as the sprite for one cursor shape

request.description:
Issued by the shell (or a helper it spawned) to register `surface` as the visible sprite the compositor should use the next time `wp_cursor_shape_device_v1.set_shape(shape)` fires on any pointer.
The compositor caches `{shape -> surface, hotspot}` and applies it lazily on the next set_shape — there is no per-pointer targeting in this protocol; cursor sprites are global to the compositor (single-seat is the only shape qdwin supports for cursor-shape). On set_shape with no cached entry the compositor falls back to its solid-colour sprite path (gated by QDWIN_CURSOR_SPRITE_SOLID).
The surface MUST NOT carry an xdg role; only the wl_surface + wl_buffer attach + commit cycle is required. The compositor owns the surface lifetime once registered: a destroy of the wl_surface (or the wl_client that owns it) clears the cache entry automatically and the shape re-falls back.
Calling with a NULL `surface` clears the cached entry for that `shape` (and falls back to solid / nothing).
`shape` values follow `wp_cursor_shape_device_v1.shape` (1..ALL_RESIZE). Out-of-range raises `invalid_shape` per cursor-shape-v1's rules.
Hotspot is in surface-local coordinates; values outside the committed buffer are clamped on apply.

arg.name: surface
arg.summary: cursor sprite surface (null clears the entry)

event.name: selection_set
event.description:
Fires whenever the seat's selection_data_source changes — i.e. a client called wl_data_device.set_selection on the seat. Used by the shell to gate cross-silo clipboard transfers (spec/10) before any destination client gets the offer.
`seat_name` matches the name reported on `seat_created`; callers correlate against their seat-tracking state.
`source_handle` is the toplevel handle of the focused window when the selection was set (the source client). Wayland only permits clients with keyboard focus to set selection, so this is unambiguous in practice. UINT32_MAX (0xffffffff) when the selection was set without a focused toplevel (e.g. by an XWayland helper or compositor-internal source) — the shell treats this as "admin" silo by default.
`mime_types_concat` packs all advertised MIME types in a single newline-separated string (LF only, no CRLF). qdshell splits and forwards to the broker. Empty string means a pre-mime-add selection — broker returns a decision regardless and the shell may re-evaluate when types arrive (selection_set re-fires on each set_selection call, including the rare no-op case).
`is_primary` is 0 for the regular Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V clipboard and 1 for the middle-click primary selection (per primary-selection-unstable-v1). Both gate through this same event but the shell may apply different default policies.
For pre-v11 shells this event isn't sent; selections behave exactly as in stock libweston (every focused client can set and any focused client can read).

request.name: clear_selection
request.description:
Sent by the shell after a deny verdict from the broker. Causes the compositor to drop the seat's selection (and the primary selection, when `is_primary=1`) — equivalent to `weston_seat_set_selection(seat, NULL, ...)`.
The destination clients see the offer disappear before they had a chance to read it, which from their perspective is indistinguishable from "the source app cleared its selection." Source apps in Qt/GTK typically log a small warning and re-set on their next user copy action.
`seat_name` MUST match a previously-emitted `seat_created` event; unknown seats are silently ignored.

event.name: activation_pending
event.description:
Fires when a Wayland client calls `xdg_activation_v1.activate(token, target_surface)`. The compositor stalls the activate (does not raise / focus the target yet) and emits this event; the shell consults broker.CheckHandoffActivation, then calls `activation_decision(handle, ...)`.
`handle` is opaque, monotonic, scoped to one pending activation. The shell MUST eventually call `activation_decision` for each handle (or destroy the shell resource); the compositor times out after 10 seconds and treats it as deny to avoid leaking pending state.
`source_handle` is the toplevel handle of the requesting client's surface (set via `xdg_activation_token_v1.set_surface` before `commit`), or UINT32_MAX if the requesting client never provided one. `target_handle` is the toplevel handle of the surface to be activated, or UINT32_MAX if the target surface has no qdwin toplevel (compositor-internal popup, etc).
`app_id` is the requesting-side `xdg_activation_token_v1.set_app_id` value, may be empty.
Pre-v12 shells don't see this event; the compositor falls back to the legacy auto-allow path.

request.name: activation_decision
request.description:
Decision values: 0 = allow — compositor proceeds with the activate (raise + focus target). 1 = deny — compositor drops the token without acting. 2 = defer — equivalent to deny for the current activate, but also signals that the shell is firing a separate `RequestPermission` so admin can approve next time.
`reason` is logged for audit; not shown to the requesting client (xdg-activation has no failure-feedback channel).
Calling with an unknown `handle` is silently ignored.

event.name: toplevel_security_context

description.summary: in-band sandbox identity for a toplevel

event.description:
Fires immediately after `toplevel_added` for any toplevel whose backing wl_client carries a `wp_security_context_v1` tag (committed via `qdwin_secctx`). Lets the shell classify sandboxed toplevels by the engine that created them (e.g. `waypipe`, `qdistro.tier2`) and the app-id the engine propagated, instead of relying on the title-prefix heuristic the tier-3 wrapper used before §6.10 shipped.
If the toplevel's client has no secctx tag, this event is not sent. Shells must treat its absence as "unsandboxed." For sandboxed clients all three string args are non-NULL but any of them MAY be the empty string if the sandbox engine chose not to set that field at commit time — e.g. `set_instance_id` is optional in the upstream protocol.
The event is also replayed on `bind_as_shell` for every already-mapped sandboxed toplevel, after the toplevel_added replay burst.

event.name: seat_focus_changed

description.summary: keyboard focus moved on this seat

event.description:
Fires whenever weston_keyboard's focus surface changes for a tracked seat — including focus loss (no surface focused) and focus restoration after a lock/unlock cycle. Shells use this for spec/10 §"focus-aware selection clear" — when focus moves to a different silo, the active selection should be dropped so the newly focused client can't `wl_data_offer.receive` the previous silo's clipboard.
`focused_handle` is the qdwin toplevel handle whose backing surface is now focused, or `UINT32_MAX` if no qdwin toplevel owns the focus (panel chrome, lock surface, RDP backend with no input delivery). Compositor-internal panels and chromes are not surfaced via toplevel_added so they always read as UINT32_MAX here, which the shell should treat as "no user-visible silo focused" — same behaviour as a real focus loss.
Pre-v14 shells don't receive this event. The compositor still tracks focus internally; it just doesn't forward it.
On `bind_as_shell` the compositor replays the current focus state once for every existing seat (after the toplevel_added burst), so the shell starts with a coherent picture without having to wait for the first user input.

arg.name: focused_handle
arg.summary: toplevel handle, or UINT32_MAX when no qdwin toplevel is focused

request.name: set_keyboard_focus

description.summary: move keyboard focus to a target toplevel

request.description:
Admin-only, ctrl-socket-style focus injection used by tests and (in future) by chrome click-to-focus. Calls `weston_keyboard_set_focus` on the target toplevel's primary view surface for every keyboard owned by `seat_name`, which emits a fresh `wl_keyboard.enter` with a new input serial — so any client that subsequently calls `wl_data_device.set_selection` with that serial wins the seat selection.
Side effect: before changing focus, the compositor calls `weston_seat_set_selection(seat, NULL, fresh_serial)` to drop any prior selection (its source's wl_client may not match the new focus and weston's stale-serial guard would otherwise reject the new client's set_selection at serial=0). The shell will then see a normal `seat_focus_changed` event for the new target.
Passing `target_handle = UINT32_MAX` clears focus (and the selection, by the same path).
Unknown seat names and unknown handles are silently ignored — the operation is best-effort and the shell can rely on the absence of a follow-up `seat_focus_changed` to detect failure.

arg.name: target_handle
arg.summary: toplevel handle, or UINT32_MAX to clear focus

event.name: data_offer_receive_pending
event.description:
spec/10 v15. Fires every time a wl_data_offer.receive is about to be honored against the seat's current selection. Lets the shell apply per-MIME / per-recipient policy in addition to the v14 focus-aware-clear gate (which is binary: all or nothing per silo).
`request_handle` is a compositor-allocated unique token; the shell echoes it back via `data_offer_receive_decision`. The token has no relation to toplevel handles or seat names — it is opaque scoped to one pending receive.
`source_handle` and `target_handle` are toplevel handles for the source-owning silo and the destination-focused silo (the wl_client that called .receive). Either may be UINT32_MAX when no qdwin toplevel maps to the side (e.g. RDP backend without delivered focus, compositor scratch surface).
`mime_type` is the exact byte string the destination requested. The shell must NOT assume canonical formatting (RFC-valid mime types only); some clients post-fix charset= parameters or use private experimental types.
`fd` is the destination's pipe write-end already dup'd into the compositor's process. The compositor RETAINS the fd until the shell decides; the shell does NOT receive it via wire. On allow the compositor invokes the source's original `send` callback with this fd; on deny the compositor closes the fd (destination sees EOF → empty paste).
If the shell does not respond within the compositor's per- pending timeout (currently ~2 s), the compositor closes the fd as if the shell answered "deny". This bounds the wedged- shell case without leaking destination fd ownership.
Pre-v15 shells: the compositor falls back to "always allow" (call source->send unconditionally), preserving v14 semantics. The shell's bound version is what the compositor consults at receive time; older shells cannot opt into the gate and the v14 focus-aware-clear remains the load-bearing defense for them.

arg.name: source_handle
arg.summary: silo that owns the data_source, or UINT32_MAX

arg.name: target_handle
arg.summary: silo that called receive, or UINT32_MAX

arg.name: mime_type
arg.summary: exact byte string requested by destination

request.name: data_offer_receive_decision
request.description:
spec/10 v15 paired request. Echoes the `request_handle` from a `data_offer_receive_pending` event with the shell's decision. `decision` is "allow" or "deny" (case-sensitive); any other value is treated as "deny" by the compositor.
Decisions on unknown handles are silently dropped — the compositor may have timed the pending out before the shell responded, or the source may have been destroyed (e.g. the owning client exited, or a fresh set_selection cancelled the prior offer). The shell should not assume side effects from a successful request.
The compositor synchronously invokes the source's original `send` (allow) or closes the destination fd (deny) before returning from this request handler. A correctly-behaving shell sends one decision per event; duplicates are safe but ignored after the first.

request.name: set_keyboard_focus_v2
request.description:
spec/10 v16. Same as `set_keyboard_focus` but the shell also names the target toplevel's silo. The compositor remembers the last `target_silo` per seat (only v2 calls update this state) and gates the unconditional pre-focus `weston_seat_set_selection(NULL, ...)` on a silo transition:
- cross-silo (target_silo != last_target_silo, OR either string is empty): clear the seat selection (and primary) before changing focus, identical to v14 behaviour. This keeps cross-silo paste-receive defense-in-depth and ensures subsequent serial=0 set_selection calls win the seat.
- same-silo (target_silo == last_target_silo, both non-empty): skip the selection clear so an active source survives the focus move. Required for the v15 sink-path: when a sink toplevel in the same silo as the source takes focus, weston sends the existing wl_data_device.selection event to the sink's wl_data_device, the sink calls `wl_data_offer.receive`, and the v15 receive-time gate fires.
After the (conditional) clear the compositor calls `weston_keyboard_set_focus` on the target toplevel exactly as in v1 of the request.
`target_silo` is an opaque string. Recommended values: "admin" for the admin uid (default uid 1000), "user1" / "user2" / ... for tier-3 silos keyed by their qdshell silo_map entry, "vm-<name>" for tier-4 libvirt domains, or any other stable identifier. The empty string means "unknown silo" and is treated as cross-silo for safety (so the clear still fires and existing v14 behaviour is preserved).
Passing `target_handle = UINT32_MAX` clears focus; the per-seat `last_target_silo` is reset to the empty string in that case so the next non-clear v2 call always counts as cross-silo.
Pre-v16 shells use `set_keyboard_focus` and do not affect the per-seat `last_target_silo` state — but the v14 unconditional clear they trigger DOES reset the running data_source, which is observable to v2 callers if they interleave the two. Don't mix v1 and v2 from the same shell; pick one based on bound version.

arg.name: target_handle
arg.summary: toplevel handle, or UINT32_MAX to clear focus

arg.name: target_silo
arg.summary: opaque silo identifier; empty means unknown (treat as cross-silo)

request.name: attach_background

description.summary: register a fullscreen wl_surface as the desktop background

request.description:
The shell creates a wl_surface sized to cover the primary output (or, in multi-output setups, one per output) and passes it here. qdwin places it on the BACKGROUND layer, replaces its compositor-owned `weston_curtain` with this surface for compositing, and reports back via the `qdwin_background_v1` handle so the shell can release / reattach.
Why: without a client surface covering the desktop, no client ever receives `wl_pointer.enter` over the empty area. That means no client can call `wl_pointer.set_cursor` for the empty desktop, which is exactly when the SPICE / VNC viewer cursor channel needs cursor data to render the pointer to the user. With an attach_background-owned surface, the shell receives pointer.enter and can call set_cursor with a default sprite — visible end-to-end.
Secondary effect: clicks on the empty desktop now have a target client surface, enabling future click-to-launcher / right-click-context-menu UX.
Pre-v18 shells continue to see qdwin's compositor curtain.

enum.name: modifier
enum.description: Mirrors libweston's `enum weston_keyboard_modifier`. The shell OR's these into the `modifier` arg of register_hotkey. Passing zero registers a hotkey with no modifier (a bare keycode).

request.name: register_hotkey
request.description:
Asks the compositor to install a key binding that fires `hotkey_pressed(id)` on this shell resource whenever the (modifier-bitmask + linux-keycode) combo is pressed and no overlay grab is active. `id` is an opaque shell-assigned token echoed back in the event.
Re-registering the same `id` is a silent replace. Modifier-only combos (key=0) are not supported and post no error; the call is a no-op.
Hotkeys do NOT fire while an overlay surface (launcher / switcher / locker) is active — those have their own grab and the shell receives input via `overlay_key`. Hotkeys are registered for the lifetime of the shell binding and torn down on shell unbind.

request.name: unregister_hotkey

description.summary: release a previously registered global hotkey

request.description: Removes the binding installed by a prior `register_hotkey` with the same `id`. Unknown ids are a silent no-op.

event.name: hotkey_pressed
event.description: Fired by the compositor when the modifier+keycode combo matching a prior `register_hotkey` is pressed. `id` is the same token the shell passed at registration. Releases are absorbed; only the press transition is reported.

event.name: chrome_button

description.summary: pointer button event over a chrome wl_surface

event.description:
Fired when a pointer button is pressed or released and the pointer focus is one of the chrome wl_surfaces the shell attached via attach_decoration. The event carries the (handle, side) of the chrome plus surface-local coords and the standard linux BTN_xxx code plus a press/release state.
Workaround for a libweston same-client gotcha: pointer events that libweston sends to surfaces owned by the same wl_client that holds the qdwin_shell_v1 binding are not reliably delivered through wl_pointer (see - same root cause that suppresses pointer.enter on shell-owned surfaces). Without this event, clicks on titlebar buttons (close, maximize, minimize) painted by the shell are never observed by the shell, so the buttons appear inert. The compositor side already knows the focused chrome view and the surface-local coordinates from its grab interface, so we forward them as a typed shell event.
Coords are wl_fixed-encoded (x256) to match wl_pointer.motion convention. button is a linux input code (BTN_LEFT=0x110, BTN_RIGHT=0x111, BTN_MIDDLE=0x112). state is 1 for press, 0 for release.
Pre-v20 shells stay on the wl_pointer path. v20 shells should ignore wl_pointer button events on chrome surfaces and rely on this event instead - otherwise a future libweston fix that restores wl_pointer delivery would cause double-fire.

arg.name: surface_x
arg.summary: surface-local x in chrome buffer space

arg.name: surface_y
arg.summary: surface-local y in chrome buffer space

event.name: popup_button

description.summary: pointer button event over an active popup surface

event.description:
Sibling of chrome_button for popup surfaces. Fired when a button event is delivered to a qdwin_popup_v1 surface owned by the shell, with the popup-local coordinates and the parent toplevel handle.
Same rationale as chrome_button: libweston cannot reliably deliver wl_pointer button events to surfaces owned by the shell client (the same-client suppression issue), so menu items inside a context-menu popup were inert before this event existed. The compositor side knows the popup is up (it owns the popup grab) and can hit-test the position against the popup view bbox, so it forwards the click as a typed shell event.
Coords are wl_fixed-encoded (x256). button is a linux BTN_xxx code; state is 1 for press, 0 for release.
The `handle` field is the parent toplevel that owns the popup. The shell dispatches on parent + popup-local y to decide which menu item was clicked.
Pre-v21 shells continue to rely on wl_pointer for popup clicks (and the menu items stay inert).

arg.name: surface_x
arg.summary: popup-local x in popup buffer space

arg.name: surface_y
arg.summary: popup-local y in popup buffer space

interface.name: qdwin_background_v1
interface.description:
Returned by `qdwin_shell_v1.attach_background`. Represents the bottom-most surface of the desktop. The shell keeps painting `surface`; qdwin positions it at the output origin and resizes via the `geometry` event on output changes.
Destroy returns control to qdwin's compositor curtain.

event.name: geometry
event.description: Fires on attach and whenever the output geometry changes. The shell resizes its wl_surface to (width, height) before the next commit.

event.name: dismissed
event.description: Compositor teardown or output disappearance. The shell should stop painting and re-attach if it wants to continue.

interface.name: qdwin_panel_v1
interface.description:
Returned by `qdwin_shell_v1.attach_panel`. Represents one panel surface pinned to a screen edge. The shell keeps painting `surface`; qdwin positions + sizes it per the anchor parameters from `attach_panel` and updates `geometry` on output changes (resize, rotate, hotplug).
Dismissed is rare — fires on compositor teardown or when the hosting output disappears. The shell should treat it as "stop painting this panel and re-attach if it wants to continue."

event.name: geometry
event.description: Fires on attach and whenever the panel's rectangle changes (output geometry, exclusive zone changes, rotation). The shell should resize its wl_surface to match (w,h) before the next commit.

event.name: dismissed
event.description: The panel's output is gone, the compositor is shutting down, or the shell's wl_surface was destroyed. The handle is inert after this fires; client should `destroy` it.

interface.name: qdwin_lock_surface_v1
interface.description: Returned by `qdwin_shell_v1.attach_lock_surface`. The surface is on the LOCK layer; compositing is gated by the `locked` state, driven by `set_locked`. Destroying the handle detaches the lock view (and, if locked, unlocks).

description.summary: compositor tore down the lock view

interface.name: qdwin_launcher_v1
interface.description: Returned by `qdwin_shell_v1.attach_launcher`. Centred on the primary output by the compositor. kind distinguishes launcher from switcher (see the request summary); the compositor treats them identically for placement.

interface.name: qdwin_notification_v1
interface.description:
Returned by `qdwin_shell_v1.attach_notification`. Represents a single compositor-placed bubble surface. The shell controls content + timeout; the compositor controls layer + corner placement.
Bubbles are composited above panels but below popups. When the hosting output goes away the compositor fires `dismissed` and the handle is inert until the client destroys it.

event.name: dismissed
event.description: Output removed, compositor shutdown, or the bubble's wl_surface was destroyed. Handle is inert after this; client should `destroy` it.

interface.name: qdwin_popup_v1
interface.description:
Returned by `qdwin_shell_v1.show_popup`. Represents one compositor-side view over the shell's popup wl_surface.
The shell owns the wl_surface and keeps painting it — qdwin re-reads on every commit. Hover feedback, item highlighting and dismiss-on-selection are entirely shell-side; the compositor's only active role is view placement, stacking, and firing `dismissed` when it decides the popup should go away (e.g. click outside).

request.name: destroy
request.description: The shell calls this after it has finished with the popup (item selected, dismissed internally, etc.). qdwin destroys the view; the wl_surface is unchanged and may be reused for another popup later.

event.name: dismissed
event.description: The compositor has decided to dismiss this popup — pointer click outside its bbox, parent toplevel closed or minimised, compositor entered locked state. The shell should respond by calling `destroy`. qdwin keeps compositing the view until destroy arrives, to avoid a frame of black where the menu was — the shell is expected to destroy on the next event- loop turn.

interface.name: qdwin_view_stream_v1

description.summary: shell-facing handle on one forwarded toplevel

interface.description:
Returned by `qdwin_shell_v1.subscribe_view_stream`. Tracks the lifecycle of one forwarded toplevel from the shell's perspective.
The shell uses this object to: - Observe approval (`approved`) with the endpoint values the compositor chose — pipewire node name, RDP port + cert, one- time password. These are typically shown to the admin as a "share this" URL / QR code. - Observe teardown (`torn_down`) so the shell can update its UI when the stream ends (subscriber disconnected, admin revoked, toplevel closed, compositor locked). - Cancel the forwarding by calling `destroy`.
Input injection from the remote RDP subscriber is NOT handled on this object — it flows through `qdwin_stream_input_v1`, advertised only to the qdistro-forward child process the compositor spawned for this stream. Splitting the trust boundary: the shell asks for forwarding; the forward proxy injects input; the compositor keeps authority over both.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Releases the pipewire output, reaps the qdistro-forward child, and restores the view to its normal output. Clients connected to the RDP endpoint see the connection drop. qdwin emits `torn_down` immediately before cleaning up so the shell sees the reason string for its own UI.

event.name: approved
event.description:
Admin approved the forward. The compositor has allocated the PipeWire output, spawned qdistro-forward, and the RDP endpoint is ready for a remote client.
`pipewire_node_name` is the PipeWire Node name (e.g. "weston.pipewire-3") suitable for `pipewiresrc path=…`.
`rdp_port` is the TCP port qdistro-forward is listening on, bound to 0.0.0.0 (or a configured bind address); the shell may build a `rdp://host:port` URL to show the user.
`rdp_cert_path` is a file path on the host to the TLS cert that qdistro-forward is serving. Needed by non-TOFU RDP clients that want to pin; sdl-freerdp with `/cert:ignore` ignores this.
`rdp_password` is a one-time password, rotated per subscribe, that the RDP client must present to connect. Prevents stray connections to the port during the subscribe window.

event.name: denied

description.summary: admin rejected or broker timed out

event.description: The subscribe did not become live. The shell should destroy this object; reusing it is an error. `reason` is a short string suitable for logging and (possibly) shell UI display.

event.name: torn_down
event.description: Emitted when the stream ends from the server side — the subscribed RDP client disconnected, the source toplevel was closed, admin revoked the approval, or the compositor entered locked state. The shell should destroy this object.

interface.name: qdwin_stream_input_v1

description.summary: remote-input injection for one forwarded stream

interface.description:
Advertised by the compositor only to the qdistro-forward child process it spawned for a given stream (identified by peer-uid plus the one-time `access_token` passed in spawn argv). No other client sees this global. This is the mechanism the remote RDP subscriber's pointer/keyboard events flow back into the compositor, scoped to a single view.
qdistro-forward calls `claim` with the `access_token` it received from argv; the compositor validates the token and binds the returned handle to the source view's per-stream `weston_seat`. Subsequent inject_* requests dispatch events through that seat. The seat's focus is locked to the source view — injection cannot leak to other views.
Tokens are one-shot and single-use. Reconnecting qdistro-forward (e.g. after a crash) requires the compositor to mint a fresh token, which currently means destroying and re-subscribing the `qdwin_view_stream_v1` on the shell side.

entry.name: invalid_token
entry.summary: access_token did not match any live stream

entry.name: not_claimed
entry.summary: inject_ request issued before successful claim

request.name: claim

description.summary: bind this connection to a pending stream

request.description: qdistro-forward calls `claim` once after connecting, with the token the compositor passed on spawn. On success, the returned handle accepts `inject_*` requests for the lifetime of the stream. On failure, `invalid_token` or `already_claimed` is raised.

interface.name: qdwin_stream_input_handle_v1
interface.description:
Returned by `qdwin_stream_input_v1.claim`. All inject_* requests on this handle are dispatched through the per-stream weston_seat whose pointer focus is locked to the forwarded view.
Coordinates for `inject_pointer_motion` are in source-view-local pixels — qdistro-forward translates from RDP-client screen coordinates as needed.
Button and key codes use Linux evdev values (BTN_LEFT = 0x110, etc., matching the values qdwin already consumes from libinput). Modifier state is layered as in xkb.

request.name: inject_modifiers
request.description: qdistro-forward computes these from the RDP wire (RDP modifier flags → xkb bitmasks) and sends them on every keyboard event; the compositor doesn't track RDP-side state.

request.name: request_frame

description.summary: ask compositor to push a PipeWire frame

request.description:
Request that the compositor schedule a repaint of the PipeWire output backing this stream, so a fresh frame is produced regardless of view damage. Used by consumers whose demand cadence doesn't match Weston's damage-driven repaint — e.g. the RDP encoder in qdistro-forward, which needs steady frames to transport to its remote client even when the source view is a static terminal.
The compositor may coalesce requests (multiple request_frame between paints collapse to a single scheduled repaint) and may defer if the output is already in a pending-repaint state. This is advisory: no guarantees about per-call frame production or latency. Rate-limit on the caller side.
